summary: Writes down current practices for complaint feedback loops, where mailbox providers tell senders when users mark mail as spam. It is based on work from the Messaging Anti-Abuse Working Group, not the IETF itself. The goal is to clarify how providers and receivers should use such feedback. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: When a user marks a message as spam, the mailbox provider that received it has no agreed way to tell the person who sent it, so abuse goes unremarked. This RFC describes the arrangements providers and senders use to close that loop, and the habits that make them work.

questions: what is a complaint feedback loop
who owns the email address in a complaint
subtitle: How mailbox providers tell senders that a user marked their mail as spam, and what both sides should do with that.

tldr.problem: When a user marks a message as spam, the mailbox provider that received it has no agreed way to tell the person who sent it, so abuse goes unremarked.
tldr.mechanism: A complaint feedback loop does exactly that: the provider sends the complaint, in a standard format, to whoever asked to receive complaints about its network.
tldr.outcome: It codifies the practices that grew up over more than a decade, for the provider side, the sender side and the people who write the automation, and it does so as a trade body's document rather than IETF consensus.

today: RFC 6449 is an Informational document published in November 2011, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It does not represent the IETF's consensus: it is a Messaging Anti-Abuse Working Group document, published as an RFC so that it would be widely available and easier to cite from other IETF work.

sections.title: How the Feedback Loop Works
sections.content:
The intent of a complaint feedback loop is to give feedback consumers the information they need to reduce spam, or the perception of spam. Feedback was originally offered only to mailbox, access and network providers, that is, to internet service providers, who would use it to spot network compromises and fraudulent accounts, or to tell a downstream customer that there may be a problem.

Senders of bulk, transactional, social or other email can use the same feedback to adjust their mailing practices, taking spam complaints as an indication that the recipient does not want to keep receiving it. Common reactions are refining opt-in practices, mailing frequency, list management and message content. Over time that has become the use most often discussed, though readers are cautioned that it is not the only one.

When an end user of a mailbox provider issues a spam complaint, the feedback provider sends a report to the feedback consumer. The report may include the full body of the original email, or, less commonly, only the full header. Some feedback providers redact information they consider private, such as the message recipient's email address.

Making sure that feedback messages go only to authorised feedback consumers is the responsibility of the feedback provider, and the identity of each message sender is generally taken from the connecting IP address of the SMTP session or from a message's DKIM signature domain, both of which are hard to forge. That matters because spammers and other miscreants also try to sign up for feedback loops on networks that do not belong to them, in order to steal email addresses and other private personal or corporate information.

Identifying the source and nature of the original message, and taking whatever action is appropriate, is the job of the feedback consumer. The feedback provider makes no claim or judgement about the validity of a complaint beyond whatever technical data it has included itself. Every complaint is forwarded without human review and without any further filtering, so some individual reports turn out not to be actionable. The consumer and the provider each judge the complaint from their own perspective and, in most cases, do not tell each other what action they took. It is also rare for any party to communicate further with the end user who started the complaint.
sections.plainLanguage: The user presses the spam button, the mailbox provider passes the complaint on to whoever asked to hear about complaints from its network, and that person decides what to do. Nobody checks the complaint first, and nobody usually tells the user what happened.

sections.title: The Vocabulary
sections.content:
The glossary separates roles that are often the same company. A mailbox provider hosts email mailboxes; an access provider gives end users access to the internet, and may or may not be the same organisation. The feedback provider sends the feedback messages, usually on behalf of a mailbox provider, and in some cases operates solely on behalf of the message recipient. The feedback consumer receives them, usually on behalf of the message originator, which is the sender but not necessarily the author. The end user is the customer of the mailbox or access provider who complains. A feedback message is a single message, usually in the Abuse Reporting Format, and a feedback stream is the set of such messages sent from one provider to one consumer.

The document deliberately avoids the acronym FBL for feedback loop, and uses ARF for the Abuse Reporting Format, which is the standard format for feedback messages. A feedback loop is also sometimes called a complaint feedback loop.

Several email terms are given precise meanings. The full header section is the whole set of header fields of a message, most of which mail user agents never show but which carry diagnostic information for automatic processing. The full body is the whole body of the message, and images and other attachments are part of it. The envelope sender is the address given in the SMTP MAIL command, and the return path header, when present, points at it. A message is considered delivered once the receiving mail transfer agent has accepted it, whatever filtering happens afterwards. Reverse DNS is the name that resolves from an IP address, and the query returns a PTR record rather than an A record.

Most importantly, the document defines spam as any message that the recipient chooses to complain about, regardless of the intent of its author or sender, and a spam complaint as the same thing. That definition is what makes the feedback useful: it is a statement about the recipient's wishes, not a judgement about the sender's conduct.
sections.plainLanguage: The glossary separates the company that hosts your mailbox from the company that passes complaints on and the company that receives them, because those are often the same company doing different jobs. It also defines spam simply as whatever the recipient complains about.

sections.title: The Mailbox and Feedback Provider Side
sections.content:
Deciding to run a feedback loop should not be taken lightly: the benefits are great, but success depends on a sound plan, an organised implementation and upkeep. The main benefits for other providers are that they are quickly alerted to spam outbreaks on their networks. End users are becoming more comfortable with reporting spam, and a feedback loop closes the loop, so the complaint reaches the message originator, who is not necessarily the sender and may be a spammer. The mail system operator is left as a messenger, relieved of the job of reviewing and forwarding complaints by hand.

Because complaints go out immediately, without review, the consumer gets them in near real time. A consumer that pays attention to its stream and acts on it receives less spam, blocks less legitimate mail, and does not have to assign staff to follow up with the originating network. A consumer that does not act may find its mail blocked or filtered by the provider, which regards the feedback as sufficient notice.

Collecting complaints. The provider needs near-real-time complaints from its users, typically by integrating the feedback mechanism with the collection of spam reports. These are usually made with a Report Spam button in a webmail interface or a proprietary desktop client, and the RFC suggests usability studies with average users before any interface change, plus a help page explaining what the button does. If the provider does not offer such a button, its chances of running an effective feedback loop are slim: asking customers to forward unwanted mail to a central address produces a low success rate, and even complete reports are hard to parse because variations in formatting and content type force the automation to be updated for each one.

Creating reports. Messages should use the Abuse Reporting Format, for uniformity and ease of processing, which also lets the provider automate generation, sending and analysis of complaint statistics. Feedback loops are usually keyed to the last hop IP address, the address that passed the unwanted message to the provider's servers, so the provider has to read the header of each complaint to find it. A provider may also supply other information, such as delivery statistics or spam trap hits, and each message should carry contact information so the consumer can ask questions, ideally feeding a ticketing system.

Policy and privacy. Information relayed from end users to a third party may need review, and anything deemed private has to be removed before it is distributed, following local policy: the recipient's or reporter's email address and IP address might be classified as private data. Privacy laws and corporate data classification standards should be consulted. Information the consumer supplies when enrolling, such as contact addresses, must also be kept private and used only for the purposes agreed at enrolment. Feedback loops inevitably cross borders, so local laws on domestic and international data exchange need to be considered; in some European countries data exchange requires permission from a governing body.

A written terms of use agreement should be provided by the provider and agreed before any feedback is sent. Four ideas belong in it: the data goes to one approved entity and not outside it, with any misuse leading to immediate termination; the consumer must keep the information it provides accurate and current; receiving feedback is a privilege that entitles the consumer to no special sending privileges; and enrolment is a privilege that can be denied or revoked at any time and for any reason.

Handling requests to receive feedback. There should be a streamlined application process with vetting, which may be stringent where the provider ties its program to a whitelist. Vetting may cross-check that the requester is authorised to receive feedback for the addresses concerned, gather other information such as whether the addresses are a smarthost network, a web hosting farm or an email marketing service, and ask for the requester's policies, contact addresses and escalation points. Enrolment is ideally a two-step process: the applicant fills in a form and must receive and acknowledge a confirmation email, best sent to abuse@ or postmaster@ at the domain in question, before the request even reaches the queue. Ownership of the addresses can and should be cross-checked through the origin autonomous system number, WHOIS records, reverse DNS of the sending hosts and other sources, which can be partly automated but often needs manual processing.

Applications may be refused, for instance where the provider suspects the requester is gaming delivery policies by creating bogus accounts and reporting false negatives to offset a bad reputation, or where the provider has already decided to block the originator's address space entirely. The provider should notify a refused applicant and keep a documented, clear and transparent appeals process, which can be as simple as replying to the refusal email asking for review.

Automation and maintenance. For the loop to be cost-effective, reports must be generatable and processable automatically, though small consumers should still be able to handle a low volume by hand. The RFC lists what to automate: accepting and validating applications, deciding whether they meet the enrolment criteria, accepting complaints from end users, producing the feedback messages and other artefacts, offering a way for consumers to engage further, and revalidating enrolments against the current criteria. Maintenance matters too, because the criteria change over time and some consumers will stop meeting them. Self-service maintenance should be offered where practicable. The provider should also send periodic probe emails to the addresses receiving feedback, as mailing list software does for subscribers, because people change employers and roles, and an invalid address means the complaints are being received and ignored.
sections.plainLanguage: The provider side is mostly about building a reliable complaint button, sending the reports in a standard format, taking care over what personal data goes out and to whom, and vetting and re-vetting who is allowed to receive complaints.

sections.title: The Feedback Consumer Side
sections.content:
A feedback consumer receives its messages once its application has been approved, and usually has subscriptions with several providers whose streams may be in different formats or carry different information. It should have a process for sorting what arrives and acting on it. A provider or access provider uses the feedback to spot network compromises, fraudulent accounts and policy violations, and the loop gives real-time visibility of complaints from recipients. A bulk sender uses the complaints to decide what to do about future mailings, by changing frequency, branding, opt-in practices or list management.

Preparation. Before asking for feedback, a consumer needs the role addresses such as abuse@ and postmaster@, and access to them, because providers often send a confirmation link to those addresses to stop users, spammers or competitors signing up for feedback they are not entitled to. It also needs a dedicated address to receive the messages, such as fbl@example.com, which is not required but makes the reports easier to handle, a list of the IP addresses it wants feedback for, with proof that it owns them, and contact details. The provider may require that the reverse DNS of each address shares the domain of the applicant or of the receiving address, and that the WHOIS information for the addresses is obviously associated with the domain. One more thing is worth knowing: if an application form asks for a credit card number or other financial information, it is assuredly a scam.

What arrives. There are three kinds. Feedback reports are the main emails: each time a recipient presses the spam button, the system creates a boilerplate report with a copy of the original message attached. Administrative messages go to the address given for the person who applied rather than the one handling the reports, and are sent infrequently but irregularly, so they should go to a role account that feeds a ticketing system or is exploded to several responsible people, since a message to an individual is easily lost when that person is on holiday or leaves. Report cards are human-readable summaries of traffic levels and complaint rates, broken down by source address or otherwise, sent regularly or when a complaint rate reaches a level worth investigating. Their content varies widely between providers, and there are no standard machine-readable formats, so they are a reference overview for a sender to monitor, and sometimes the only warning before mail is blocked altogether.

Handling a complaint. The expectations boil down to three things. Where the consumer controls the sending, it should not send mail of the same type to that recipient again. It should identify the underlying problem, if any, and fix it so fewer reports of that kind arrive. And it need not tell the provider or the end user what action it took.

Unsubscription and suppression. A sender of commercial email should treat a feedback message much like an unsubscribe request, making sure no further email from that list reaches the recipient, either by removing the address from the list or adding it to a suppression list. How broadly to apply that needs judgement: suppressing the address across an entire email service is probably too broad, but if one consumer has several segmented lists, suppressing across all of them is probably right. Not all complaints are intentional, since recipients hit the wrong button or mark a whole mailbox as spam, but the best default is to assume the recipient does not want more mail and suppress it in all but fairly extreme cases, such as a list the recipient pays to receive, email from a genuine company to its own employees, or email from a provider to its users. Transactional mail is more complicated: for a receipt or a bill, the right thing may be to contact the recipient through another channel, or in rare cases to ignore the complaint, because suppressing an airline ticket confirmation the customer wanted would only annoy them. In all these cases the goal is to keep the customer happy and reduce future complaints, even where that means ignoring the feedback.

Trending and reporting. Counting the messages over regular periods gives useful information. A sudden increase from a particular customer or server may mean a spammer has signed up or a system has been compromised. Ten complaints a day would be a sign of serious trouble in some cases but perfectly normal for a sender that sends 300,000 emails a month, so the count has to be judged in context. An email service provider can break the data down further, by customer, list or campaign, and can divide complaints by the number of emails sent, which is often a more useful metric than the absolute count. Two traps are worth knowing. Complaints are usually counted on the day they were sent, which is the day the message was read, so a sender that mails Monday to Friday sees a high complaint rate on Saturday, when few emails were sent and the rate can exceed 100%. And if an organisation sends 10,000 emails of which perhaps 500 reach the inbox, dividing 10 complaints by 10,000 gives a respectable 0.1%, while the provider dividing by the 500 delivered to the inbox gets 2%, which is grounds for blocking. A large gap between a reported complaint rate and one calculated from raw delivery numbers is worth investigating.

Automation. Even when signing up is partly automated, changes tend to be handled by hand, and even changing the address that messages are sent to is time-consuming. Every consumer should create a unique email alias for each feedback loop, even if they all deliver to the same inbox at first: it makes the source of a report obvious, allows lightweight pre-processing, and makes discarding a stream easy. A consumer expecting to scale up, or to outsource processing, may prefer a subdomain for its feedback streams. Small consumers with lists of a few thousand recipients, or small providers with no history of problems, can manage reports by hand, since an ARF message should be readable in most mail clients, though a tool such as arffilter can annotate the subject line with the address being reported to make patterns easier to spot.

Larger consumers need automation, and the main capability is extracting the relevant data reliably: the recipient of the original email, the mailbox provider that sent the report, the customer that sent the original email, the campaign and list it belonged to, and possibly the sending IP address and its DKIM signature domain. That is hard without doing some work before the email is sent, because providers redact addresses in the To: header and delete identifying information wherever they can; identifying the user from the Message-ID, subject line and received timestamps needs access to the mail server logs, is painful, and is only worth doing in an exceptional case. The solution is the one used for automated bounce handling with VERP: embed the information in the email so that it is unlikely to be stripped but easy to recognise. It may already be there as VERP in the return path, or in a one-click unsubscribe link in the body; if not, the local part of the Message-ID is a good place, because that is often used to track a message through delivery and is available in the logs. A database key is small and opaque but needs database access to resolve; encrypting the information inside the email removes that need but still needs some automation. A hybrid, storing the pieces separately and encrypting or obfuscating some of them, is a compromise: a Message-ID of esp-423-27-42460@example.com is opaque to a third party but someone familiar with the format can tell it is from customer 423, campaign 27, recipient 42460. Once such identifiers are embedded, a processor can extract them with a regular expression and a couple of database queries, then suppress the address and record the customer and campaign for reporting. If delivery data is stored in a form that matches the VERP string used for bounces, the feedback processor can create a fake hard bounce and hand it to the existing bounce processor to suppress the address.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiving side has to have the right addresses set up before it asks for complaints, treat each complaint like an unsubscribe request, fix whatever caused it, and, once the volume is too big to read, work out which recipient each report is about from identifiers hidden in the original mail.

sections.title: The Report Format and the Appendices
sections.content:
Appendix A traces the Abuse Reporting Format. The first feedback loop to be deployed, the scomp system at AOL, sent an entire copy of the message to the consumer and assumed large consumers would embed enough information in the email to identify which recipient had complained. That worked while there was only one provider offering feedback, but as more mailbox providers joined it became useful for the provider to add further information, machine readable and human readable, to the report. That led to ARF, which quickly became the de facto standard and is now used by nearly all feedback providers and constitutes the vast majority of feedback messages worldwide. ARF was later published by the IETF as RFC 5965, and there are no competing standards for reporting individual messages.

An ARF report is sent by email, one message for each spam report, in a standard MIME format called multipart/report with three sections. The first holds human-readable plaintext, mainly for small consumers handling reports by hand: boilerplate explaining that this is a feedback message, with links to contact details and other data. The second holds machine-readable information, including the version of the ARF protocol used and the type of report, such as abuse or fraud, and possibly optional details such as the original envelope sender or the time the mail was received. In theory that section could be used to route and triage the report mechanically, but in practice most feedback messages are treated identically, and consumers who prefer to work from the third section ignore it entirely. The third section is a copy of the original email, as a message/rfc822 attachment; it will often be modified or redacted, especially the recipient's email address, for privacy or legal reasons.

Appendix B explains using DKIM to route feedback. Historically the last hop IP address, the mail transfer agent that passed the message into the receiving provider's domain, was the only reliable identifier for the source of a message. DKIM adds another: the authenticated domain, which is the d= value in the DKIM-Signature header. In a social sense, signing a message is a statement of responsibility for it. A DKIM signature is usually applied by the author or originator, which may be far upstream of the last hop, and that matters when a recipient forwards to another address: users with chains of forwarding accounts cannot complain effectively, because their provider cannot follow the message back to the original sender. A single d= value may be used across many servers and addresses, and servers come and go without changing it, so a feedback loop based on DKIM needs no reconfiguration when addresses change, unlike one based on IP addresses. One recurring concern is that email service providers send messages addressed with hundreds of thousands of customer domains but want feedback for all of them; DKIM removed the tie between d= and the From header that its predecessor DomainKeys had, so an email service provider can sign with a domain of its own and sign up for feedback on everything signed with it.

Appendix C asks whether a provider may set up a feedback loop for a consumer that never asked for one. There is continuing debate, and the working group neither endorses nor condemns it, but if a provider does it, the guidelines are that it should only be for mailbox and access providers, only after trying to contact the provider and ask whether a loop can be set up normally, and only sending to the published abuse address from the provider's WHOIS record. The arguments for include that consumers may not realise they have abuse problems until complaints start arriving, that they may not know feedback loops exist, that upstream providers gain another stream for spotting problem customers, and that sending reports of abuse back to the provider automates the process. The arguments against include that it confuses consumers who did not apply, that it can conflict with existing terms of service, since a provider with a policy of terminating service after a number of complaints may be forced to act on complaints it never asked for, that upstream providers cannot see the mail their customers send and so cannot tell whether bulk complaints are a real problem, that the listed abuse address may not be the right place for automated complaints, that it may feed a ticketing system that cannot handle ARF messages, and that consumers may not be equipped for the volume or the format.
sections.plainLanguage: The appendices cover the report format itself, how a signed domain can stand in for an IP address as the identifier, and whether a provider may start sending complaints to someone who never asked for them.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Considerations
sections.content: The document says security and privacy considerations are discussed in many of its sections, most notably the overview, the section on policy concerns and the section on handling requests to receive feedback. The threads running through them are these. The identity of a feedback consumer has to be checked, because spammers try to sign up for loops on networks that do not belong to them in order to steal email addresses and other private personal or corporate information. The data in a complaint may contain private information, such as the reporter's email address and IP address, and has to be removed before it goes to a third party. The information a consumer supplies when enrolling is private in turn, and may only be used for the purposes agreed at the time. Because feedback loops cross national borders, local laws on data exchange apply, and in some countries data exchange requires permission from a governing body. The terms of use should say that the data goes only to the approved recipient, that it must not be passed on, that receiving it is a privilege that brings no special sending rights, and that enrolment can be revoked at any time.
sections.plainLanguage: Three things matter for safety here: checking who is allowed to receive complaints, stripping anything private out of the complaints themselves, and keeping the enrolment information to the agreed purpose.

viz.caption: WHAT A FEEDBACK CONSUMER SHOULD DO WITH A COMPLAINT

items.title: Treat it like an unsubscribe
items.text: Remove the address from that list, or add it to a suppression list.

items.title: Fix the cause
items.text: Find and fix the underlying problem so fewer reports of that kind arrive.

items.title: Suppress in most cases
items.text: Assume the recipient wants no more mail, except in fairly extreme cases.

items.title: Transactional mail needs judgement
items.text: For receipts and bills it may be right to ignore the report, or to contact the recipient another way.

items.title: No need to reply
items.text: There is no need to tell the provider or the user what you did.

items.title: Track the rate, carefully
items.text: Count complaints against mail delivered, but check for the weekend and inbox traps.
